source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276:247-254
finding: Three of six wild crows learned a two-trap tube, kept avoiding the trap when arbitrary colour cues were removed, then solved a visually different trap-table problem at once. The authors say this makes chance, associative learning, visual and tactile generalisation and prior dispositions unlikely.
numbers: 6 crows; 3 solved the tube (Obo, Tiga, Slevin), mean 103.3 +/- 20.3 trials; 3 failed within the 150-trial cap. Trap-table pass rule 15/20 (alpha 0.05); all 3 solvers passed and chose right on trial 1. The 3 non-solvers failed the trap-table. Solvers avoided the trap on 10 of 12 first trials.
limits: Only 3 successful subjects. Learning was slow (over 100 trials). All 3 solvers FAILED Transfer 3 (functional trap plus an open hole with no base; probability that all three peak in side-switching there by chance p = 0.0156), so the reasoning is partial. Non-solvers differ possibly by inhibitory control, not causal insight.
agent_relevance: Template for G3: a control is not one test but a ladder of transfers that strip each shortcut cue in turn (colour cue removed, shape changed, material changed), plus a hard negative the true mechanism would still fail or pass in a specific way.

source: Taylor, Roberts, Hunt, Gray (2009) Causal reasoning in New Caledonian crows: ruling out spatial analogies and sampling error. Commun Integr Biol 2:311-312
finding: Two rival explanations of the trap-table transfer were tested. Sampling bias: naive crows did not avoid the trap on the table. Spatial analogy: crows facing an inverted tube with the hole on the top surface showed no end preference.
numbers: Sampling bias test: 8 naive crows, 20 trials each (two blocks of 10, trap side alternated); none above chance (all binomial p > 0.05). Across 14 crows tested on the trap-table (8 naive + 6 original), only the 3 trap-tube solvers passed. Inverted tube: 3 solvers, none showed a significant end preference.
limits: Exact p-values and the trial count for the inverted tube are not reported in the addendum. Still n = 3 for the key claim.
agent_relevance: After a transfer result, run a naive-baseline arm (no prior training) and a rule-flip arm. The naive baseline shows the held-out item is not solved by default dispositions alone.

source: Jacobs, von Bayern, Martin-Ordas, Rat-Fischer, Osvath (2015) Corvids create novel causal interventions after all. Proc R Soc B 282:20142504
finding: Reply to Taylor et al. (2014), who found crows could not make novel causal interventions while 2-year-olds could. The reply lists confounds that make the crow-versus-child comparison unfair: prior experience, familiarity, apparatus complexity, a visible ledge that could act as a cue, fixed position of the effective hole, and unclear transparency of the apparatus.
numbers: Taylor et al. 2014 as reported: crows got food in 100/100 observation trials and 0/100 experimental trials; children needed about 3 observation and 3 experimental trials. No new data in the reply.
limits: Commentary without new experiments. Subject counts are not given in the reply.
agent_relevance: A failure also needs controls: a negative result (agent 'cannot do X') can come from format, cue salience or apparatus complexity. G3 checks should include a task-format control before concluding a capability is absent.

source: Taylor, Knaebe, Gray (2012) An end to insight? New Caledonian crows can spontaneously solve problems without planning their actions. Proc R Soc B 279:4977-4981
finding: A horizontal two-string task (one string connected to meat, one broken) removes the food-moves-closer feedback. Humans solved it; crows did not, which favours a perceptual-motor feedback loop over insight for string pulling.
numbers: Humans: 49/50 correct in Exp 1, 42/50 in Exp 2 (p < 0.00001). Crows: 11 birds; first trial 8/11 connected (p = 0.11); one bird 13/20 (p = 0.13); the other 10 chose connected on 16/25 (p = 0.11) and none pulled enough to move food. Pooled preference p = 0.037, no individual significant.
limits: Pooled significance was judged a likely fluke by the authors. Crows quit after few trials, so low motivation without feedback, not lack of understanding, is a rival reading.
agent_relevance: Remove the intermediate feedback signal and see if the behaviour survives. For our agent: if success depends on a checker's partial signal at each step, test the same task with the signal withheld to learn whether the plan or the feedback loop did the work.

source: Taylor et al. (2010) An investigation into the cognition behind spontaneous string pulling in New Caledonian crows. PLoS ONE 5
finding: With visual feedback restricted, experienced string-pullers lost much of their efficiency, while naive crows mostly failed. This was read as support for operant conditioning via a perceptual-motor loop rather than insight.
numbers: 12 crows in 3 groups of 4 (experienced, naive, mirror). Experienced group pull-step ratio fell from 96.5 +/- 1.86% to 55.7 +/- 10.1%; errors about 10 times higher (one-tailed Wilcoxon p = 0.0625). Naive: 1 of 4 solved. Mirror: 2 of 4 solved (6 of 10 trials each). Naive vs experienced U = 16, p = 0.0286; mirror vs experienced U = 10, p = 0.6857.
limits: n = 4 per group; the smallest possible Wilcoxon p with n = 4 is 0.0625, so none of the key tests can reach 0.05. Authors call the conclusion tentative.
agent_relevance: Shows how small-N designs cap evidence. For our held-out checks, plan enough items that a single test can actually reach significance; do not report a pass on a check that cannot fail.

source: Logan, Jelbert, Breen, Gray, Taylor (2014) Modifications to the Aesop's Fable paradigm change New Caledonian crow performances. PLoS ONE 9:e103049
finding: Eight crows on water-displacement variants. Most chose sinking and solid objects, but success on the covered U-tube did not transfer to the uncovered version, which points to a learned colour-cue association instead of a model of the hidden mechanism.
numbers: 8 crows, 20 trials per experiment. Sinking vs floating: all 6 passed, 85% sinking. Solid vs hollow: all 6 passed, 95% solid. Wide vs narrow equal levels: 4 of 6 passed, 64% narrow. Unequal levels: 3 of 4 passed, 79% wide. Coloured U-tube: only 1 bird passed, 47% connected overall. Uncovered U-tube: 0 of 5 passed, 44% connected. First-trial correct 15/17 for Exps 1-3 (p = 0.002) but 5/10 for volume and U-tube.
limits: Small n (4-6 per test), many incomplete. A solid-object preference resembling stones may confound earlier studies. Feedback from visible food movement not ruled out for the volume task.
agent_relevance: Variant ladder: same logic, new surface. A pass on the cued version and a fail on the uncued version marks cue learning. Build held-out checks as an uncued twin of each training item.

source: Miller, Jelbert, Taylor, Cheke, Gray, Loissel, Clayton (2016) Performance in object-choice Aesop's Fable tasks are influenced by object biases in New Caledonian crows but not in human children. PLoS ONE 11:e0168056
finding: Crows had strong pre-existing object biases (sinking, solid) that coincide with the functional choice, which inflates apparent understanding. When the bias was set against function, crows chose non-functional but rewarded objects. Children's choices were not changed by bias training.
numbers: 5 crows; 29 of 30 insertions sinking and 29 of 30 solid before training (p < 0.0001). Sinking-vs-floating trial 1: crows 24% sinking, children 67%. Trials 1-5: crows 31%, children 80%. Passed criterion: crows 0/5 and 0/5; children 13/29 (45%) and 5/33 (15%). When rewarded for non-functional items crows dropped 49 non-functional vs 3 functional on trial 1 (p < 0.0001). Children: 29 aged 5-9 and 33 aged 5-10.
limits: Authors do not claim crows lack causal understanding; inhibition problems and untested visual feedback remain rival readings.
agent_relevance: Check whether the correct answer coincides with a default preference of the solver. A held-out item must make the default choice wrong, as here, or a pass says nothing. Directly relevant to G3 and to model priors toward the common answer.

source: Neilands, Jelbert, Breen, Schiestl, Taylor (2016) How insightful is 'insight'? New Caledonian crows do not attend to object weight during spontaneous stone dropping. PLoS ONE 11:e0167419
finding: Signature-testing: look for a specific error the rival theory predicts. If crows understood force they would drop heavy blocks first; if they only copy beak contact they would ignore weight. The two crows that spontaneously dropped blocks made the weight inattention error, yet after training all others chose heavy blocks.
numbers: 12 crows. Pre-test: no weight preference (128 of 240 trials light; p = 0.167). Only 2 of 12 crows innovated dropping. D4R dropped heavy 12 times vs light 22 (p = 0.062). After training, 125/140 first choices heavy (p < 0.001); three birds scored 10/10 at once.
limits: Only 2 spontaneous innovators. Lower innovation rate than the original von Bayern study; the authors suggest beak insertion in the earlier set-up may explain it.
agent_relevance: The best design in this set: choose a variable the two theories disagree about (weight) and test the error signature. For our agent: pick the property a shortcut would ignore and make a held-out item turn on it. Also shows the capacity was present when probed after training, so a single failed probe is not proof of absence.

source: Jelbert, Miller, Schiestl, Boeckle, Cheke, Gray, Taylor, Clayton (2019) New Caledonian crows infer the weight of objects from observing their movements in a breeze. Proc R Soc B 286:20182332
finding: Crows watched novel objects blown by a fan, then chose which to drop. They picked the right object first well above chance with the fan on and at chance with the fan off. The paired fan-off control rules out unintended visual cues in the objects.
numbers: 12 crows (6 trained on light-rewarded, 6 on heavy-rewarded). First touch correct: 35/48 (72.9%, p = 0.01) fan on vs 23/48 (47.9%, p = 0.34) fan off. Very first test: 11/12 correct with fan on (p = 0.003) vs 6/12 off. First drop correct 44/48 (92%) on, 38/48 (79%) off. Effect of condition on touching the incorrect object: chi2 = 15.76, p <= 0.001. No effect of rewarded object type.
limits: Few tests per bird by design (to prevent learning). Drops were high in both conditions, so the touch measure carries the effect. No evidence of what the birds represent beyond weight.
agent_relevance: Good model of an alternative-explanation control: the same objects, counterbalanced, with the single informative cue switched off. Counting the very first trial per item guards against learning during the test.

source: Gruber et al. (2019) New Caledonian crows use mental representations to solve metatool problems. Curr Biol 29
finding: Three-stage tool problems with each stage hidden from the others plus distractor tools were meant to rule out chaining and perceptual-motor feedback. Crows reached criterion, which the authors read as pre-planning of three behaviours.
numbers: Exp 1: criterion 16/20 within 40 trials (alpha 0.015). 11 crows got the stick problem then the stone problem; several reached criterion only in 40-46 trials; none of the three 2017 crows given the stone problem first reached criterion within 40 trials, yet they reached it in 22, 23 and 24 trials on the stick problem second. Exp 2 (shortcut trials; 8 crows) allowed up to 120 trials.
limits: Order effect shows prior experience helps; 'first conclusive evidence' is the authors' wording and rests on a handful of birds and 40-120 trial learning, so training could leave room for learned rules.
agent_relevance: Distractor items that look useful but are not (a tool in the wrong place) are the hidden-stage analogue of a poisoned example. Use distractors in held-out checks to separate planning from local chaining.

source: Boeckle et al. (2020) New Caledonian crows plan for specific future tool use. Proc R Soc B 287:20201490
finding: Crows learned a temporal rule with novel tools, then chose tools to match an apparatus they would see later. Novel tool-apparatus pairings in the test were used to rule out reliance on a preferred tool or natural repertoire.
numbers: Training: 4 of 6 crows reached criterion in 20-25 trials (Neptune 17/20, Saturn 19/23, Triton 18/21, Uranus 19/25). Test conditions 3-4: 3 of 4 above chance (Neptune 9/10, Triton 7/10, Uranus 7/10; Saturn 3/10, p = 0.429; five-way choice). Learning effect in training significant only when the two non-passers are excluded (trial z = 2.155, p = 0.031). No learning effect in test.
limits: Only 4 birds tested. 4 of 9 passed initial training. The paper's text mentions nine individuals while six were reported in the results table.
agent_relevance: Test items use combinations never seen in training, and the answer flips with the condition. Good pattern: if the best response changes with a manipulated upstream fact, a fixed habit cannot explain it.

source: Bastos et al. (2021) Kea (Nestor notabilis) fail a loose-string connectivity task. Sci Rep 11
finding: Kea solved the standard vertical string task within the first couple of trials but chose at chance between a connected and a disconnected string, as the perceptual-motor feedback loop view predicts and the insight, planning and means-end views do not.
numbers: 7 kea, 20 trials each; correct first touch 10/20, 11/20, 12/20, 9/20, 7/20, 7/20, 11/20 (all Bayes factors under 0.7, i.e. no support for above-chance). Attempted switches in 41 of 140 trials (29.3%), 9 in the wrong direction. Strings fully retrieved in 112/140 trials. Exp 2: 7 of 8 kea retrieved the token; first-trial duration 71.36 +/- 42.88 s vs 8-10 s on later trials (previous study 83.10 +/- 128.39 s; BF10 = 0.705).
limits: Small group; some failures could reflect motivation. Fits crow results (b04), so this is a cross-species replication of the null.
agent_relevance: A same-day pass on an easy variant and a chance result on a matched hard variant is the signature of a feedback shortcut. Pair every 'solves the task' claim with its matched-difficulty twin that removes the shortcut.

source: Bastos and Taylor (2020) Macphail's null hypothesis of vertebrate intelligence: insights from avian cognition. Front Psychol 11:1692
finding: Reviews the rival general-process (associative learning only, equal intelligence across species) view and argues avian work shows both species differences and behaviour not explained by associative learning alone. Reflects on limits of comparative psychology and suggests strategies for progress.
numbers: Review; no new numbers. Cites the trap-tube, string-pulling and Aesop's fable work covered in b01-b12.
limits: Authors are from the same lab as many cited studies, so the case is partly self-assessment.
agent_relevance: The framing 'default to the simpler explanation until a test discriminates' is the null hypothesis G3 should encode: the cheaper explanation (cue use, pattern match) stands unless a held-out test rules it out.

source: Taylor, Miller, Gray (2012) New Caledonian crows reason about hidden causal agents. PNAS 109:16389; with commentary by Dymond, Haselgrove, McGregor (2013) and reply by Taylor, Miller, Gray (2013) PNAS
finding: The original study found more vigilance toward a hide when a hidden agent could still be present. A commentary said the human-agent trials always came before the unseen-agent trials, and the conditions differed in number of people, timing, location and stick movement. The reply argued that falling inspection rates over trials 1-3 showed habituation, so order could not explain the result.
numbers: Reply reports no new statistics, only trial range 1-3 and the one-person vs two-person difference. Original study had 8 subjects (as shown in O'Neill 2021, b15).
limits: Fixed condition order meant order effects and condition differences were confounded. The reply's argument does not remove that confound.
agent_relevance: Fixed order and bundled differences between arms are the typical hole in a control. In our held-out arms, counterbalance order and change one thing at a time.

source: O'Neill et al. (2021) Do New Caledonian crows reason about hidden causal agents? A replication revisited. Animal Behavior and Cognition 8(2):166-189
finding: A replication with a new set of crows plus three control groups answering the commentaries did not reproduce the original effect. Because the base effect failed, the extra control groups could not be interpreted, and the paper says it neither supports nor refutes hidden-agent reasoning.
numbers: 14 crows in four groups: direct replication n = 4, counterbalanced replication n = 4, associative-cue control n = 3, counterbalanced cue control n = 3. Replication: hide inspections per minute HCA 8.69 (SD 1.1) vs UCA 10.95 (SD 2.31), paired t(3) = -2.16, p = .12. Reverse order: HCA 7.52 vs UCA 9.26, t(3) = -0.93, p = .42. Original study had 8 subjects.
limits: With n = 4 per group the study cannot separate low power from a true difference.
agent_relevance: A failed replication leaves all control arms uninterpretable. For our harness: first confirm the base effect on the held-out set, only then read the ablation arms.

source: Kano et al. (2017) A test of the submentalizing hypothesis: apes' performance in a false belief task inanimate control. Commun Integr Biol 10:e1343771
finding: Heyes proposed that apes' anticipatory looks in the false-belief task came from low-level cueing (e.g. the green shirt acting as a retrieval cue). The inanimate control replaced the human actor with a mirrored object. Apes made fewer anticipatory looks and showed no tendency to look to the 'correct' location.
numbers: Control: 43 apes; 22 of 43 (51.16%) looked at a box in the anticipatory phase vs 22 of 30 (73.33%) in the original. First looks to target: 14 of 22 (p = 0.28, two-tailed binomial); FB1 6 of 11 (p = 1.0); FB2 8 of 11 (p = 0.23).
limits: Absence of an effect with the inanimate control argues against submentalizing but does not prove mentalizing.
agent_relevance: The canonical example of a rival-hypothesis control: keep the low-level stimulus features, remove the property under test, and see whether the effect disappears. A model of an 'agent' effect can be tested with a surface-matched control with no agent.

source: Miller et al. (2020) Decision-making flexibility in New Caledonian crows, young children and adult humans in a multi-dimensional tool-use task. PLoS ONE 15:e0219874
finding: Across species, children and orangutans over-used tools when not needed, while adult humans, cockatoos and crows did not; crows and children could not refrain from non-functional tools; birds struggled when two apparatuses, two tools and two reward qualities varied at once.
numbers: Abstract-level only: comparison of 3-5-year-old children, adult humans and NC crows, with earlier orangutan and Goffin cockatoo data. Specific counts were not extracted.
limits: Counts not recorded in this record, only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Moderator: performance drops when several variables vary together. Held-out checks should vary one dimension at a time first, then combine, to see where a solver collapses.

source: Lapuschkin, Waldchen, Binder, Montavon, Samek, Muller (2019) Unmasking Clever Hans predictors and assessing what machines really learn. Nat Commun 10:1096
finding: A Fisher vector image classifier scored well on horses by reading a source tag present in about one fifth of the horse images. Removing the tag removed the ability to classify horses; inserting it on a car image changed the classification. Explanation heatmaps exposed the shortcut.
numbers: Tag present in about one fifth of horse pictures (PASCAL VOC 2007). No overall accuracy figure was extracted here.
limits: Image classifier, not a language model. Shows the shortcut only after looking inside the model.
agent_relevance: Machine analogue of the animal Clever Hans control: edit the suspected cue (remove, insert elsewhere) and watch the output. This is the mutate-input check named in G3.

source: Wu, Qiu, Ross, Akyurek, Chen, Wang, Kim, Andreas, Kim (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks. NAACL
finding: Eleven tasks with a default and a counterfactual version (e.g. base-9 addition, 1-based indexing, altered word order, chess openings with swapped pieces). Four models score above chance on counterfactuals but fall substantially below their default scores, so part of the skill is tied to the default world.
numbers: Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2; temperature 0. Arithmetic: 1,000 two-digit sums per base (8, 9, 10, 11, 16); gaps sometimes go 'from near-perfect to near-zero'. GPT-3.5 parseable programs drop from 99% (default) to 62%, 71% and 75% for the flipped and rotated settings. Counterfactual comprehension checks (CCC) are run in each task.
limits: Temperature-0, prompt-sensitive; execution budget may matter (in-context learning still leaves a sizeable gap). Models can still do the counterfactual above chance.
agent_relevance: The CCC is the key design: a separate easy probe showing the model understood the counterfactual rule, so a drop cannot be blamed on misreading the instructions. Use it with every held-out mutation in G3. Also tells us the counterfactual twin should be built into the harness.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models. CogSci
finding: Webb et al. (2023) claimed GPT-3 matches humans on letter-string analogies. With permuted alphabets and symbol alphabets, the models do worse while humans stay high, and GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are no better than GPT-3. Error types differ from human errors.
numbers: Each data point is the mean of 70 samples (ours) vs 100 samples (Webb); 95% binomial confidence intervals. Models: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Comprehension checks show models understand the permuted alphabet in general (GPT-3.5 has trouble with 'predecessor'). Webb et al. had 57 UCLA undergraduate participants.
limits: Zero-generalisation problems only; exact accuracy numbers not extracted here beyond the pattern.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a published 'LLM matches humans' result may depend on training-set familiarity. Held-out checks should use re-keyed alphabets, shuffled symbol mappings and similar re-codings.

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. arXiv 2308.16118
finding: Two objections to Webb et al.: zero-shot cannot be assumed when problems may be in the training data (the authors acknowledged this in the review file), and tests built for humans may not measure LLMs. Simplest variations of the tasks broke GPT-3 while human performance stayed high.
numbers: Variations include larger letter intervals and randomly shuffled alphabets; GPT-3 performed poorly on both. Exact figures were not extracted.
limits: Short response paper; appendix results are small-scale.
agent_relevance: Same message as b20 from an earlier date: 'novel' must be checked, not assumed. Contamination risk is a rival explanation to rule out for any LLM pass.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks. arXiv 2302.08399
finding: Minor changes to a false-belief vignette that keep the logic (transparent container instead of opaque, so the character can see the contents) flip the model's answers. The paper argues the zero hypothesis for model evaluation should be skeptical and that outlying failures should outweigh average success.
numbers: Transparent bag variant: the model still says Sam believes the bag holds chocolate with probability 95% (popcorn 0%), though she can see popcorn; for the second belief prompt popcorn 58% vs chocolate 36%.
limits: Single model family tested, small set of vignettes, not a large benchmark; author notes changes to the paper between versions.
agent_relevance: A single principled failure beats a high average, as in animal work. G3 should treat one logic-preserving mutation failure as disconfirming evidence, not noise.

source: Shapira, Levy, Alavi, Zhou, Choi, Goldberg, Sap, Shwartz (2023) Clever Hans or neural theory of mind? Stress testing social reasoning in LLMs. arXiv 2305.14763
finding: Six theory-of-mind tasks plus adversarial variants. Models show some ability, but it is not robust; they struggle on adversarial examples, which points to shallow heuristics.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy 97% on the original false-belief subset, but fails on adversarial transparent-access and relationship-change samples. TriangleCOPA 96% by flan-t5-xxl (near solved). ToMi: GPT-3.5 81% best overall, lower on belief questions. SocialIQa: GPT-4 79% total vs 61% on 'others effect' subset in one place of the paper and 74.5% in another place (text inconsistent).
limits: Numbers vary within the paper text; the SocialIQa 'others' figure is inconsistent between two passages. Models tested are from early 2023.
agent_relevance: Match each benchmark with an adversarial twin. The gap between original and twin, not the original score, is the number to track.

source: Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Shahrokhi, Tuzel, Bengio, Farajtabar (2025) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in LLMs. ICLR 2025
finding: Templates regenerate GSM8K questions with new names and numbers. Accuracy drops on GSM-Symbolic across models and varies widely across instantiations. Changing names matters little, changing numbers matters more, more clauses lowers accuracy and raises variance. Adding an irrelevant but plausible clause (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops.
numbers: GSM-NoOp drops of up to 65% across state-of-the-art models. Original GSM8K scores sit close to the distribution seen when only names change. o1-preview applied an irrelevant 10% inflation detail in a worked example.
limits: Template-generated problems may differ in difficulty from the originals; exact per-model drops were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready test kit for G3: randomise numbers, add a distractor clause, add clauses. Report a distribution over instantiations, not one score.

source: Zhang, Da, Lee, Robinson, Wu, Song, Zhao, Raja, Zhuang, Slack, Lyu, Hendryx, Kaplan, Lunati, Yue (2024) A careful examination of LLM performance on grade school arithmetic (GSM1k). NeurIPS Datasets
finding: A freshly written 1,000-question set (GSM1k) matched to GSM8k in difficulty reveals contamination: several model families drop by up to 8%. The gap correlates with the model's probability of generating GSM8k items. Even the most overfit models still solve much of the new set.
numbers: Accuracy drops up to 8%; Spearman r2 = 0.36 between probability of generating GSM8k examples and the GSM8k-GSM1k gap. Phi-2 loses 6% yet still solves over half of GSM1k, similar to Llama2-70B.
limits: Drop is modest for most models; the correlation is moderate (r2 = 0.36); contamination is not the only reason for the gap.
agent_relevance: The fix for contamination is a held-out set written after the model's cutoff by independent authors, with human-solve-rate matching. A cheap version for our agent: write fresh checks after any training or prompt tuning.

source: McCoy, Yao, Friedman, Hardy, Griffiths (2023/2024) Embers of autoregression: understanding LLMs through the problem they are trained to solve. arXiv 2309.13638
finding: Accuracy follows the probability of the task, the target output and the input even in deterministic tasks where probability should not matter. A cipher decoding example shows the size of the effect.
numbers: GPT-4 decoding a simple cipher: 51% when the output is a high-probability word sequence vs 13% when low-probability. Eleven tasks with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
limits: Two models from 2023. The effect is a trend; it does not say which tasks are affected in newer models.
agent_relevance: Control for output probability: matched held-out items where the right answer is a rare form. If accuracy tracks surface frequency, the pass is partly a prior.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language models don't always say what they think: unfaithful explanations in chain-of-thought prompting. NeurIPS
finding: Biasing features (e.g. reorder multiple-choice options so the answer is always A) change model answers but are not mentioned in the chain of thought, which rationalises the biased answer. Accuracy drops by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0; accuracy drop up to 36% under biasing; social-bias task explanations justify stereotyped answers without mentioning the bias.
limits: Early models; the explicit bias manipulations are artificial.
agent_relevance: An alternative-explanation control for the agent's own reasoning text: edit a cue in the input and test if the written reasoning changes. If not, do not accept the reasoning as the cause (supports G2 and the 'written reasoning is not a record' rule).

source: Kim, Sclar, Zhou, Le Bras, Kim, Choi, Sap (2023) FANTOM: a benchmark for stress-testing machine theory of mind in interactions. EMNLP
finding: Multiple question types that need the same underlying reasoning are used to expose an illusory sense of ToM; the benchmark builds consistency checks into the design.
numbers: Abstract-level only; no per-model numbers were extracted from the PDF text in this session.
limits: Only the abstract was read closely.
agent_relevance: Design idea: ask several differently phrased questions that require one underlying inference, score a pass only if all agree.

source: Gandhi, Franken, Gerstenberg, Goodman (2023) Understanding social reasoning in language models with language models (BigToM). NeurIPS
finding: Procedurally generates ToM evaluations from causal templates, with 25 controls and 5,000 model-written evaluations; humans rated the quality above earlier crowd-sourced sets and comparable to expert-written ones.
numbers: 25 controls, 5,000 evaluations (abstract). Model-vs-human numbers were not extracted.
limits: Abstract-level; the generator is itself an LLM, so its tests can share blind spots with the models tested.
agent_relevance: Templates with controls built in make it cheap to produce many held-out mutations; check generator independence from the model under test (G4).

source: Cross-study synthesis of b01-b16 (animal alternative-explanation controls)
finding: The controls that held up were those that (1) removed the proposed shortcut cue while keeping the task logic, (2) set the default preference against the correct answer, (3) tested a signature error the rival theory predicts, (4) used a naive or inanimate baseline, and (5) counted first trials. Those that fell short had fixed condition order, n of 3-4, or could not produce a significant result at all.
numbers: Examples: trap-table needed 3 of 6 solvers; naive baseline 0 of 8; hidden-agent study replication 0 effect with 4+4+3+3 crows; string pulling Wilcoxon p floor 0.0625 at n = 4.
limits: My own synthesis; not a source. Most animal studies have n between 3 and 14, so effect sizes are weakly bounded.
agent_relevance: Maps to G3 checklist: strip-the-cue twin, default-against-answer item, signature-error item, naive baseline, first-attempt scoring, counterbalanced order, sample size large enough for the test to be able to fail.
